label: Money and Provision
framing: Scripture treats money as a matter of the heart, where the treasure is, there the heart will be also. It does not condemn the thing but warns that the love of it, not the having of it, is a root of every kind of evil.
cultural: In the ancient world wealth was visible, tied to land and household, and the poor had no safety net but the community and the law that left them the gleanings of the field. The Bible's relentless concern for the poor was a scandal to an empire that despised them, and its warnings to the rich named exactly whom their hoarding starved.
historical: The early church startled Rome by sharing its goods and feeding the poor. Across the centuries, figures from Basil of Caesarea, who built a city for the poor in the fourth century, to John Wesley, who told Christians to gain all they can and give all they can, have read these texts as a call to the open hand.
application: Hold your money as a steward, not an owner. Give a set portion first, before the rest of your spending bends around it, and watch what generosity does to the grip of fear. Avoid the schemes that promise wealth without work, and gather little by little. A good name is to be chosen over great riches.

verses.text: Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
verses.where: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus turns from prayer and fasting to possessions with the same logic: what is stored with God lasts, and what is stored for this world does not. Verse 21 gives the reason in one line. Money follows the heart, and the heart follows the money.

verses.text: No one can serve two masters: Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.
verses.where: The section on possessions reaches its verdict with the picture of a servant and two masters. Money is not treated as a neutral tool here but as a master that asks for loyalty. Jesus does not say a person may not have money; he says money cannot be served alongside God.

verses.text: And He said to them, “Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.”
verses.where: A man in the crowd asks Jesus to make his brother split an inheritance. Jesus refuses to judge the dispute, warns everyone listening against every form of greed, and tells the parable of a rich man who builds bigger barns on the night his life is required of him.

verses.text: You might say in your heart, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.” But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth, in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers even to this day.
verses.where: Moses speaks to Israel before it enters a rich land. The danger he names is not poverty but plenty: full houses and growing flocks, and a heart that forgets and says its own hands made the wealth. Remembering that God gives the power to gain wealth is the guard against pride.

verses.text: He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth is never satisfied by income. This too is futile.
verses.where: The Teacher has just watched officials exploit the poor, and now he looks at money from the inside. The one who loves it is never filled by it. Everyone leaves the world as naked as he came, carrying nothing from his labor.

verses.text: Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these.
verses.where: Paul is writing about teachers in Ephesus who treated religion as a way to make money. The moral philosophers of his day praised contentment as needing little; Paul uses the same word but grounds it in God, who gives food and clothing, and in the plain fact that we brought nothing into the world.

verses.text: Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy. Instruct them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share, treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
verses.where: Wealthy believers in Ephesus would have been expected to fund public buildings and feasts in return for honor and inscriptions. Paul turns that expectation toward God: the rich are not to be proud or to hope in wealth, but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share.

verses.text: Jesus looked at him, loved him, and said to him, “There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.”
verses.where: A man who has kept the commandments asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus looks at him and loves him before he names the one thing lacking: sell what you own, give to the poor, and follow. The man goes away grieving, and Jesus tells his stunned disciples that what is impossible for people is possible with God.

verses.text: But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.”
verses.where: Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector in Jericho, rich from a trade that cheated its neighbors. Jesus invites himself to his house before Zacchaeus promises anything. The answer comes as deeds: half his goods to the poor, and fourfold repayment to anyone he cheated.

verses.text: Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver.
verses.where: Paul is gathering a gift from Greek churches for poor believers in Jerusalem. He uses the farmer's picture of sowing, and asks for giving that is decided in the heart, not squeezed out by pressure. The harvest he promises is more capacity to be generous, so that thanks goes to God.

misread.taken: The verse is often quoted as “money is the root of all evil”, either to make money itself sound dirty or, more often, to wave the whole subject away as something only greedy people need to hear.
misread.says: Paul does not say money is evil, or that it is the only root of evil. He says the love of money is a root from which every kind of evil can grow. The word he uses means fondness for silver, and he aims it at people who wanted to be rich, some of them religious teachers. The warning is not addressed to the very rich alone. Anyone can crave money, and Paul says that craving has led people away from the faith and into many sorrows.
misread.text: For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.

misread.taken: The promise to “open the windows of heaven” is used to teach that giving a tenth, or giving to a particular ministry, is a way to guarantee a larger financial return.
misread.says: Malachi is speaking to Judah under the law of Moses. The tithe fed the Levites, who had no land, and through the temple storehouse it fed the poor; withholding it starved both. God's challenge to test him is a call to trust him in a hard season, and the blessing he names is rain and harvest for a farming people. Christians differ on how tithing applies today, but no faithful reading turns this verse into a technique for getting rich.
misread.text: Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house. Test Me in this,” says the LORD of Hosts. “See if I will not open the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing without measure.

misread.taken: Sayings like this one are used to teach that poverty is always the result of laziness or weak faith, and that wealth is proof of diligence and God's favor.
misread.says: Proverbs describes how life usually goes: diligence tends toward plenty, idleness toward want. It is a true generalization, not a verdict on every poor person. The same book says that the field of the poor can be swept away by injustice (Proverbs 13:23), and Job and Ecclesiastes stand in the Bible to say the pattern has exceptions. Using this verse to blame the poor goes against the book it comes from.
misread.text: Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth.

whole: Money rarely presents itself as a spiritual problem. It shows up as a mortgage, a raise that disappeared into new spending, a quarrel at the kitchen table, a quiet sense of being behind everyone else, or a quiet sense of being ahead and deserving it. Most people think about money far more than they pray about it, and many Christians have heard two messages from the church that cancel each other: that money is dirty, and that God wants to make them rich. Neither helps a person decide what to do with next month's paycheck.

Scripture speaks about money often, and almost never in the abstract. It treats wealth as a real good from God's hand, something to enjoy and share (1 Timothy 6:17), and it treats the love of wealth as one of the most dangerous loyalties a human heart can hold. Jesus speaks of money as a rival master, which means the question is not first how much a person has but who is being served. Deuteronomy saw the danger before Israel ever got rich: plenty makes people forget, and forgetting turns into the boast that our own hands did it. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes saw the other side of the same trap. Love money, and it will never be enough.

That is why the Bible's remedy is not a budget rule but a different loyalty. Contentment, in Paul's sense, is not grim self-denial; it rests on the God who provides and on the fact that nothing comes with us at the end. Generosity follows from it, not as a fee paid to God but as the natural shape of a heart that has stopped being owned. Zacchaeus shows what that looks like when it happens all at once: no one tells him to give, but once Jesus has come into his house, the money goes out of it, and justice to the people he cheated comes first.

None of this lets anyone off. The rich man who went away sad had kept the commandments, and Jesus still asked for the thing he could not release. Most readers in the comfortable world are richer than they feel, and the Bible's warnings about wealth were written for people with far less. The honest question is the one Jesus asked through that man's story: what would I refuse to give up if he asked? That question is not answered once. It is answered in ordinary choices about spending, saving, giving and debt, made before God, with the poor kept in view.

differ.share: Christians agree that everything a person has comes from God, that greed is a serious sin, that the poor are to be cared for, that generosity belongs to the Christian life, and that wealth is never by itself a sign of God's favor.

views.name: Stewardship of what you hold
views.body: Many Christians read Scripture as allowing believers to own property, earn, save and build, provided they hold it as stewards accountable to God, give generously, and refuse to let it rule them. On this view the ordinary Christian life of work, saving for a family and giving faithfully is a right use of wealth.

views.name: Simplicity as a calling
views.body: Other Christians, among them those in the monastic orders who take vows of poverty and many in the Anabaptist tradition, hold that Jesus' words to the rich man and the sharing of the first church in Acts call at least some believers to a deliberately simple life, and call every church to question its comfort.

views.name: How much to give
views.body: Christians also differ on giving. Many churches teach the tithe, a tenth, as the starting point; others read the New Testament as asking for generous, cheerful giving in proportion to what a person has, without a fixed percentage (2 Corinthians 8:12, 9:7).

differ.after: All of them teach that money is a servant and a test, never a master, and all of them reject the teaching that giving is a way to get rich. The Honest Answer “What does the Bible say about money?” sets out the question at more length.

deep.sit: If someone read your last three months of spending without knowing you, what would they say you love, and is that what you would say?

prayer.lead: A prayer from the longest psalm, asking God to turn the heart before the hand.
prayer.text: Turn my heart to Your testimonies and not to covetous gain. Turn my eyes away from worthless things; revive me with Your word.
